chunks: And from him, from Ibrahim ibn Hashim, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he heard him saying:

"Indeed, Al-Anfal are lands where there was no shedding of blood, or people who were reconciled and gave with their own hands. As for lands that are desolate or the bellies of valleys, all of this is from Al-Fay'. And Al-Anfal are for Allah and the Messenger (peace be upon him and his family). What is for Allah is for the Messenger (peace be upon him and his family), and he places it where he wills."

key_terms.أَرْضٍ خَرِبَةٍ: Desolate lands, uncultivated or unused land
key_terms.الْأَنْفَال: Plunder or booty, specifically lands conquered without fighting or through reconciliation
key_terms.الْفَيْء: Expropriated property or wealth acquired without battle
key_terms.صُولِحُوا: They were reconciled, referring to peace treaties where people submitted voluntarily
key_terms.هِرَاقَةُ دَمٍ: Shedding of blood, referring to military conquest through combat

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between Anfal and Fay in Shia Islamic jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the jurisprudential distinction between *Al-Anfal* (war booty from conquest or reconciliation) and *Al-Fay* (expropriated property from desolate lands or valleys), a key topic in Chapter 39 regarding supplementary rulings. It establishes that while both categories ultimately belong to Allah and the Messenger, the Prophet holds the discretionary authority (*mashī'a*) to allocate them, a principle that later Shia jurists extended to the Imam in the Occultation. This distinction underscores the divine ownership of territorial gains and the central role of the Imam in managing communal resources.
